title: Semantic satiation
hook: Say a word enough times and it turns into a strange, meaningless sound.
peek: Repeat a word out loud thirty times, any word, and it starts to sound foreign, then like noise. Psychologists have a name for this, coined in a 1962 doctoral thesis at McGill University.
lede: Pick a word, say 'spoon', and repeat it aloud for half a minute. Somewhere along the way it stops feeling like a word. It becomes a strange noise your mouth is making, and you may briefly wonder if it is spelled right. The effect was described in 1907, and the name semantic satiation came from a 1962 thesis by Leon Jakobovits James at McGill.

bullets.text: Two American psychologists had people stare at a printed word for minutes at a time. Many said it began to look strange and lose its meaning, the same effect seen rather than heard.
One leading explanation is that the brain's response to a repeated word briefly fades, so its meaning feels weaker. Rest a few moments and the meaning comes back.

bullets.opening: Taking the sting out of words
bullets.text: Jakobovits James suggested that repetition might also dull the emotional charge of a loaded word, and some therapists have borrowed the idea for anxious thoughts. The evidence for it is modest.
